study.title: Revelation 17 The woman, the beast, and the judgment of God
study.overview: Revelation 17 shows, in symbolic language, the divine assessment of a corrupt power that seduces nations, pursues the saints and looks dominion, but is destined for ruin. The chapter contrasts the deceptive splendor of the woman and the beast with the sovereignty of the Lamb and the fact that God directs to the movements of his enemies. The text also explains that the political and religious attraction of this system reaches peoples and rulers, but their appearance of stability does not prevent their end.

outline.title: The invitation to see the trial of the great whore
outline.explanation: One of the angels calls John to contemplate the sentence of the woman who is on many waters. It represents spiritual infidelity and influence over kings and peoples, who get drunk with their corruption.

outline.title: The appearance of the woman and her identity of blood and luxury
outline.explanation: John sees the woman mounted on the scarlet beast, adorned with wealth and ostentation, but holding a cup full of impurity. Her name reveals that she is the mystery of the great Babylon, associated with the perversion of the earth and the blood of the saints.

outline.title: The angel explains the mystery of the woman, the beast and the kings
outline.explanation: The vision is interpreted: the beast had a story of ascension and fall and walks toward perdition; the heads and horns point to kingdoms and kings; all unite against the Lamb, but the Lamb wins as Lord of lords, and his followers are called, chosen and faithful.

outline.title: The waters, the betrayal of the allies and the domination of the great city
outline.explanation: The waters are peoples and nations; the beast's own allies end up hating the woman and desolate her, but this also happens within the purpose permitted by God. The chapter ends by identifying the woman with the great city exercising royalty over the kings of the earth.

study.context: The notes link the scene to the power of Rome in John's time, especially for his reach on trade routes and centers of power, and for his responsibility in the persecution of Christians. This identification is presented by the commentators as interpretation, not as explicitly named in the biblical text. The chapter also dialogues with the biblical image of prostitution as infidelity to God and drunkenness as uncontrolled surrender to corruption.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that evil can present itself with beauty, wealth and authority, but continues to be spiritual infidelity and violence against the people of God. The seduction of kings and nations shows that idolatry has a public, political and religious dimension at the same time. The beast seems invincible, but its trajectory is already marked for perdition. The central point is the victory of the Lamb: Christ not only resists his enemies, but overcomes them because he is the sovereign Lord. At the same time, God remains in control of history, using even the perverse unity of enemies to fulfill his words. Believers appear as called, chosen and faithful, that is, belonging to the Lamb and not to the seductive system of the world.

scholarViews.insight: The Ample waters indicate the wide range of Rome's power over peoples and trade routes; the comment reads this as the basis of the seductive domination of the great whore.
The woman is described as unfaithful to the covenant with God and drunken the kings of the earth with her spiritual prostitution, the image of religious and moral corruption.

The commentator understands that the woman assembled in the beast represents a church or idolatrous religious system, and reads the image of the cup as a sign of abominable errors disseminated to the peoples.

questions: What signs of the chapter show that the religious or political splendor can hide corruption before God?
How will the assertion that the Lamb will win changes the way of facing powers that seem dominant?
How can a Christian community remain faithful when the surrounding environment presses for alliances and concessions?
study.practice: Read this chapter as a call to vigilance against the seduction of power, wealth and public approval. Examine whether there are areas in which faith has been mixed with practical idolatry, trust in human structures, or tolerance to sin to gain advantage. Instead of admiring what impresses, choose fidelity to the Lamb in concrete attitudes: truth, purity, courage and perseverance. Also practice hope: evil may seem organized and strong, but the text ensures that its end is already decided by God.
study.uncertainty: There are relevant interpretative differences in the notes regarding the exact identity of the woman, the beast and the great city. Tyndale and Matthew Henry relate the image mainly to Rome and the persecutive power of their time; Adam Clarke proposes a reading linked to the Latin Church. The biblical text, however, uses symbols that allow discussions beyond what is explicitly named, so these identifications should be treated as interpretations, not as indisputable conclusions.
